claim: Beetle elytra are hardened forewings primarily serving as protective covers for the hindwings and body underneath.
source: We chose beetle elytra—hardened forewings primarily serving as protective covers for the hindwings and body underneath—to perform the morphological disparity analysis for three reasons: (1) elytra are the most commonly preserved fossils of Palaeozoic and Mesozoic beetles, and they are easily accessible in the literature and in online databases; (2) Permian and Triassic elytra display complex morphological structure (Ponomarenko, 1969); (3) elytra morphology has long been studied in relation to taxonomic diversity of living and extinct beetles (Ponomarenko, 2004; Tong et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is stated directly in the manuscript and represents established knowledge.

claim: Permian trace fossils showing wood boring provide convincing evidence for the xylophagous habit of ancient beetles.
source: Moreover, Permian trace fossils showing wood boring provide convincing evidence for the xylophagous habit of these ancient beetles (Naugolnykh and Ponomarenko, 2010; Feng et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Naugolnykh and Ponomarenko, 2010 and Feng et al., 2019.

claim: Aquatic or semi-aquatic beetles including Phoroschizidae and Ademosynidae, belonging to the suborder Archostemata, first appeared in the Middle Permian and diversified in the Late Permian.
source: Aquatic or semi-aquatic beetles including Phoroschizidae and Ademosynidae, belonging to the suborder Archostemata, first appeared in the Middle Permian and diversified in the Late Permian (Ponomarenko, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ponomarenko, 2003.

claim: The three other suborders of Coleoptera, comprising Polyphaga, Adephaga, and Myxophaga, most likely evolved by the Late Permian, but definite fossils are rare at this time.
source: The three other suborders of Coleoptera, comprising Polyphaga, Adephaga, and Myxophaga, most likely evolved by the Late Permian, but definite fossils are rare at this time.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the fossil record.

claim: Permian beetles probably played an important ecological role in forest ecosystems because most Permian beetles were most likely xylophagous insects that consumed living and dead woody stems.
source: Permian beetles probably played an important ecological role in forest ecosystems because most Permian beetles were most likely xylophagous insects that consumed living and dead woody stems (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from morphological and trace fossil evidence, supported by Figure 3.

claim: Some Permian xylophagous beetles fed on living wood tissues.
source: Some Permian xylophagous beetles fed on living wood tissues (Feng et al., 2017; Feng et al., 2019), which likely reduced tree productivity and could have caused extensive tree mortality.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Feng et al., 2017 and Feng et al., 2019.

claim: Permian xylophagous beetles feeding on living wood tissues likely reduced tree productivity and could have caused extensive tree mortality.
source: Some Permian xylophagous beetles fed on living wood tissues (Feng et al., 2017; Feng et al., 2019), which likely reduced tree productivity and could have caused extensive tree mortality.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the feeding behavior of these beetles.

claim: Insect-mediated tree mortality is known to result in large transfers of carbon from biomass to dead organic matter.
source: Insect-mediated tree mortality is known to result in large transfers of carbon from biomass to dead organic matter (Seidl et al., 2018; Fei et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Seidl et al., 2018 and Fei et al., 2019.

claim: Other Permian xylophagous beetles were likely saproxylic (feeding on dead wood).
source: The other Permian xylophagous beetles were likely saproxylic (feeding on dead wood) (Ponomarenko, 2003), and they could also impact terrestrial carbon dynamics by accelerating wood decomposition (Ulyshen, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ponomarenko, 2003.

claim: Permian saproxylic beetles could impact terrestrial carbon dynamics by accelerating wood decomposition.
source: The other Permian xylophagous beetles were likely saproxylic (feeding on dead wood) (Ponomarenko, 2003), and they could also impact terrestrial carbon dynamics by accelerating wood decomposition (Ulyshen, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ulyshen, 2018.

claim: Saproxylic animals first appeared in the Devonian and are mainly represented by small invertebrates such as oribatid mites, until the Permian.
source: Saproxylic animals first appeared in the Devonian and are mainly represented by small invertebrates such as oribatid mites, until the Permian (Labandeira et al., 1997; Labandeira, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Labandeira et al., 1997 and Labandeira, 2007.

claim: Grazing by micro- and meso-invertebrates (nematodes, collembolans, enchytraeids and oribatid mites) did not significantly affect wood decomposition.
source: Whereas grazing by micro- and meso-invertebrates (nematodes, collembolans, enchytraeids and oribatid mites) did not significantly affect wood decomposition, consumption by macro-invertebrates (dominated by saproxylic beetles and termites in modern ecosystems) significantly sped up wood decomposition (Tapanila and Roberts, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tapanila and Roberts, 2012.

claim: Consumption by macro-invertebrates (dominated by saproxylic beetles and termites in modern ecosystems) significantly sped up wood decomposition.
source: Whereas grazing by micro- and meso-invertebrates (nematodes, collembolans, enchytraeids and oribatid mites) did not significantly affect wood decomposition, consumption by macro-invertebrates (dominated by saproxylic beetles and termites in modern ecosystems) significantly sped up wood decomposition (Tapanila and Roberts, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tapanila and Roberts, 2012.

claim: Permian saproxylic beetles are likely to have had a variety of indirect effects on decomposition, including creating tunnels that facilitate the movement of fungi into wood.
source: In addition to those that directly facilitated decomposition by consuming wood, Permian saproxylic beetles are likely to have had a variety of indirect effects on decomposition, including creating tunnels that facilitate the movement of fungi into wood (Naugolnykh and Ponomarenko, 2010; Feng et al., 2017), and vectoring fungi and other decay organisms on or within their bodies, like their extant counterparts (Ulyshen, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Naugolnykh and Ponomarenko, 2010 and Feng et al., 2017.

claim: Permian saproxylic beetles likely vectored fungi and other decay organisms on or within their bodies, like their extant counterparts.
source: In addition to those that directly facilitated decomposition by consuming wood, Permian saproxylic beetles are likely to have had a variety of indirect effects on decomposition, including creating tunnels that facilitate the movement of fungi into wood (Naugolnykh and Ponomarenko, 2010; Feng et al., 2017), and vectoring fungi and other decay organisms on or within their bodies, like their extant counterparts (Ulyshen, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ulyshen, 2016 and inference from modern beetles.

claim: Permian beetles that feed on living and dead wood probably could impact terrestrial carbon dynamics by reducing forests' carbon sequestration capacity, and by converting live materials to dead organic matter and subsequent decomposition.
source: In conclusion, Permian beetles that feed on living and dead wood probably could impact terrestrial carbon dynamics by reducing forests' carbon sequestration capacity, and by converting live materials to dead organic matter and subsequent decomposition.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the feeding behavior and ecological role of Permian beetles.

claim: The oxygen concentration of the atmosphere began to rise in the early Palaeozoic, probably with a peak in the Carboniferous and large decline from the beginning of the Permian.
source: The oxygen concentration of the atmosphere began to rise in the early Palaeozoic, probably with a peak in the Carboniferous and large decline from the beginning of the Permian (Dahl et al., 2010; Berner, 2009; Krause et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dahl et al., 2010; Berner, 2009; and Krause et al., 2018.

claim: The reason for the Permian decline in atmospheric oxygen was attributed to a tectonic- or climate-driven reduction in the extent of coal swamps.
source: The reason for this plunge was attributed to a tectonic- or climate-driven reduction in the extent of coal swamps (Berner and Canfield, 1989) or to the evolution of lignin-consuming fungi (Floudas et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Berner and Canfield, 1989.

claim: The reason for the Permian decline in atmospheric oxygen was attributed to the evolution of lignin-consuming fungi.
source: The reason for this plunge was attributed to a tectonic- or climate-driven reduction in the extent of coal swamps (Berner and Canfield, 1989) or to the evolution of lignin-consuming fungi (Floudas et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Floudas et al., 2012.

claim: Global recoverable coal is only equivalent to a few percent of the oxygen budget in the atmosphere, and thus cannot account for the large drop of atmospheric oxygen.
source: However, global recoverable coal is only equivalent to a few percent of the oxygen budget in the atmosphere, and thus cannot account for the large drop of atmospheric oxygen (Nelsen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nelsen et al., 2016.

claim: Lignin-consuming fungi may have been present before the Carboniferous.
source: Furthermore, lignin-consuming fungi may have been present before the Carboniferous (Nelsen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nelsen et al., 2016.

claim: A new geochemical model proposed that the development of Permian terrestrial herbivores may have limited transport and long-term burial of terrestrial organic compounds in marine sediments, resulting in less organic carbon burial and attendant declines in atmospheric oxygen.
source: Recently, a new geochemical model proposed that the development of Permian terrestrial herbivores may have limited transport and long-term burial of terrestrial organic compounds in marine sediments, resulting in less organic carbon burial and attendant declines in atmospheric oxygen (Laakso et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Laakso et al., 2020.

claim: Herbivorous insects and amniotes are thought to be the major herbivorous animals during the Permian and thus are considered to be the most important drivers of the Permian change in biogeochemical cycles of carbon.
source: Herbivorous insects and amniotes are thought to be the major herbivorous animals during the Permian and thus are considered to be the most important drivers of the Permian change in biogeochemical cycles of carbon (Laakso et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Laakso et al., 2020.

claim: Permian herbivorous amniotes mainly fed on leaves, stems, roots, and rhizomes.
source: However, Permian herbivorous amniotes mainly fed on leaves, stems, roots, and rhizomes (Sues and Reisz, 1998; Pearson et al., 2013) and could normally digest cellulose by fermentation but could not consume lignin, as in extant herbivorous vertebrates (Pearson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sues and Reisz, 1998 and Pearson et al., 2013.

claim: Permian herbivorous amniotes could normally digest cellulose by fermentation but could not consume lignin, as in extant herbivorous vertebrates.
source: However, Permian herbivorous amniotes mainly fed on leaves, stems, roots, and rhizomes (Sues and Reisz, 1998; Pearson et al., 2013) and could normally digest cellulose by fermentation but could not consume lignin, as in extant herbivorous vertebrates (Pearson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pearson et al., 2013.

claim: The majority of terrestrial plant biomass is stored in forest woody tissue consisting of decay-resistant lignin.
source: The majority of terrestrial plant biomass is stored in forest woody tissue consisting of decay-resistant lignin (Hibbett et al., 2016; Bar-On et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hibbett et al., 2016 and Bar-On et al., 2018.

claim: In modern forests, the total carbon stock in woody tissue (including living and dead wood) is approximately 340 Pg carbon, much more than 72 Pg carbon in roots (below ground), 43 Pg carbon in foliage, and 43 Pg carbon in litter.
source: In modern forests, the total carbon stock in woody tissue (including living and dead wood) is approximately 340 Pg carbon, much more than 72 Pg carbon in roots (below ground), 43 Pg carbon in foliage, and 43 Pg carbon in litter (Reich et al., 2014; Pan et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Reich et al., 2014 and Pan et al., 2011.

claim: In extant forest ecosystems, insects may account for 29% of the total carbon flux from dead wood and thus they have a functional importance in the decomposition of dead wood and the carbon cycle.
source: In extant forest ecosystems, insects may account for 29% of the total carbon flux from dead wood and thus they have a functional importance in the decomposition of dead wood and the carbon cycle (Seibold et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Seibold et al., 2021.

claim: During the Permian, beetles were probably the dominant consumers of woody tissue, while a few other insect groups may have sometimes fed on dead wood (such as stem dictyopterans and protelytropterans).
source: During the Permian, beetles were probably the dominant consumers of woody tissue, while a few other insect groups may have sometimes fed on dead wood (such as stem dictyopterans and protelytropterans) (Grimaldi and Engel, 2005).
evidence: This claim is based on inference and supported by a citation to Grimaldi and Engel, 2005.

claim: Permian beetles had probably evolved close interactions with various microorganisms, especially lignin-consuming fungi, which also accelerated the decomposition of dead wood.
source: Permian beetles had probably evolved close interactions with various microorganisms, especially lignin-consuming fungi (Nelsen et al., 2016), which also accelerated the decomposition of dead wood.
evidence: This claim is based on inference and supported by a citation to Nelsen et al., 2016.

claim: The Early Permian onset of the decrease in oxygen concentrations is consistent with the origin and radiation of the xylophagous beetles in the fossil record.
source: The Early Permian onset of the decrease in oxygen concentrations is consistent with the origin and radiation of the xylophagous beetles in the fossil record.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the temporal correlation between oxygen decline and beetle radiation.

claim: Permian xylophagous beetles could have been responsible for at least part of the change in Permian biogeochemical cycles in Laakso's model.
source: Therefore, we propose that Permian xylophagous beetles could have been responsible for at least part of the change in Permian biogeochemical cycles in Laakso's model (Laakso et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on inference from the ecological role of Permian beetles.

claim: Extant insects have significant effects on terrestrial carbon and nutrient cycling by modulating the quality and quantity of resources that enter the detrital food web.
source: As the most taxonomically and functionally diverse group of living organisms on Earth (Stork, 2018), extant insects have significant effects on terrestrial carbon and nutrient cycling by modulating the quality and quantity of resources that enter the detrital food web (Belovsky and Slade, 2000; Kurz et al., 2008; Yang and Gratton, 2014; Seibold et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Stork, 2018; Belovsky and Slade, 2000; Kurz et al., 2008; Yang and Gratton, 2014; and Seibold et al., 2021.

claim: The effects of insects on terrestrial ecosystems in deep time have been viewed as unimportant or overlooked.
source: However, the effects of insects on terrestrial ecosystems in deep time have been viewed as unimportant or overlooked (Doughty, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Doughty, 2017.

claim: Permian beetles were among the principal degraders of wood and played a fundamental role in deep-time carbon and nutrient cycling and niche creation.
source: Permian beetles were among the principal degraders of wood and played a fundamental role in deep-time carbon and nutrient cycling and niche creation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the ecological role of Permian beetles.

claim: Insects may have been one of the major regulating factors of forest ecosystems at least from the Permian.
source: Insects may have been one of the major regulating factors of forest ecosystems at least from the Permian.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the ecological role of Permian beetles.

claim: Both the taxonomic diversity and morphological disparity dropped dramatically during the Early Triassic.
source: Our results show that both the taxonomic diversity and morphological disparity dropped dramatically during the Early Triassic (Figures 2 and 4).
evidence: This claim is stated directly in the manuscript and supported by Figures 2 and 4.

claim: All xylophagous stem-group beetles become extinct near the Permian-Triassic boundary or abruptly decreased in the Early Triassic (a pattern called 'dead clade walking').
source: Combined with the phylogenetic results (Figure 3), our suite of analyses yields a clear ecological signal from beetles across the Permian/Triassic boundary: all xylophagous stem-group beetles become extinct near the Permian-Triassic boundary or abruptly decreased in the Early Triassic (a pattern called 'dead clade walking'; Barnes et al., 2021), while aquatic phoroschizid and ademosynid lineages crossed the Permian/Triassic boundary and diversified in the Middle Triassic.
evidence: This claim is stated directly in the manuscript and supported by Figure 3 and citation to Barnes et al., 2021.

claim: Aquatic phoroschizid and ademosynid lineages crossed the Permian/Triassic boundary and diversified in the Middle Triassic.
source: Combined with the phylogenetic results (Figure 3), our suite of analyses yields a clear ecological signal from beetles across the Permian/Triassic boundary: all xylophagous stem-group beetles become extinct near the Permian-Triassic boundary or abruptly decreased in the Early Triassic (a pattern called 'dead clade walking'; Barnes et al., 2021), while aquatic phoroschizid and ademosynid lineages crossed the Permian/Triassic boundary and diversified in the Middle Triassic.
evidence: This claim is stated directly in the manuscript and supported by Figure 3.

claim: Coleoptera recovered in taxonomic diversity during the Middle Triassic by the rise of new predatory and herbivorous groups, synchronized with the recovery of terrestrial ecosystems.
source: Coleoptera recovered in taxonomic diversity during the Middle Triassic by the rise of new predatory and herbivorous groups, synchronized with the recovery of terrestrial ecosystems (Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is stated directly in the manuscript and supported by a citation to Zhao et al., 2020.

claim: The morphological disparity in the Middle Triassic is significantly lower than that of the Middle and Late Permian due to the lack of stem-group beetles that possess complex elytra structures.
source: However, the morphological disparity is significantly lower than that of the Middle and Late Permian due to the lack of stem-group beetles that possess complex elytra structures (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is stated directly in the manuscript and supported by Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Polyphagan groups increased in taxonomic diversity during the Middle Triassic, which is a transitory epoch from a Palaeozoic stem-group beetle assemblage to a Mesozoic polyphagan-dominated assemblage.
source: Polyphagan groups increased in taxonomic diversity during the Middle Triassic, which is a transitory epoch from a Palaeozoic stem-group beetle assemblage to a Mesozoic polyphagan-dominated assemblage.
evidence: This claim is stated directly in the manuscript and supported by data analysis.

claim: Xylophagous groups are absent or rare in Early Triassic coleopteran assemblages, becoming widespread again from the Middle Triassic, mainly represented by more derived archostematans (such as Cupedidae) and polyphagans.
source: Xylophagous groups are absent or rare in Early Triassic coleopteran assemblages, becoming widespread again from the Middle Triassic, mainly represented by more derived archostematans (such as Cupedidae) and polyphagans (Ponomarenko, 2003).
evidence: This claim is stated directly in the manuscript and supported by a citation to Ponomarenko, 2003.

claim: The gap in xylophagous beetles coincided chronologically with the gap in coal deposition ('coal gap'), a time during which peat-forming forests were rare or absent, extending across at least the entire Early Triassic.
source: This gap in xylophagous beetles coincided chronologically with the gap in coal deposition ('coal gap'), a time during which peat-forming forests were rare or absent (Figure 3B), extending across at least the entire Early Triassic (Benton and Newell, 2014; Retallack et al., 1996; Nowak et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is stated directly in the manuscript and supported by Figure 3B and citations to Benton and Newell, 2014; Retallack et al., 1996; Nowak et al., 2020; and Zhao et al., 2020.

claim: During the latest Permian and earliest Triassic, gymnosperm-dominated forests abruptly collapsed.
source: During the latest Permian and earliest Triassic, gymnosperm-dominated forests abruptly collapsed (Vajda et al., 2020) and were replaced by other biomes (such as isoetalean-dominated herbaceous heathlands; Feng et al., 2020) in most areas due to extreme conditions including aridity (Sun et al., 2012), wildfires (Shen et al., 2011), and ozone destruction (Benca et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vajda et al., 2020.

claim: Gymnosperm-dominated forests were replaced by other biomes (such as isoetalean-dominated herbaceous heathlands) in most areas due to extreme conditions including aridity, wildfires, and ozone destruction.
source: During the latest Permian and earliest Triassic, gymnosperm-dominated forests abruptly collapsed (Vajda et al., 2020) and were replaced by other biomes (such as isoetalean-dominated herbaceous heathlands; Feng et al., 2020) in most areas due to extreme conditions including aridity (Sun et al., 2012), wildfires (Shen et al., 2011), and ozone destruction (Benca et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Feng et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2012; Shen et al., 2011; and Benca et al., 2018.

claim: In some regions, the plant extinction was less severe, or the recovery was rapid, or there may have been multiple crises during the Early Triassic.
source: In some regions, the plant extinction was less severe, or the recovery was rapid (Hochuli et al., 2010), or there may have been multiple crises during the Early Triassic (Schneebeli-Hermann et al., 2017), but even short-term ecosystem disruption could have led to extinctions among xylophagous beetles.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hochuli et al., 2010 and Schneebeli-Hermann et al., 2017.

claim: Even short-term ecosystem disruption could have led to extinctions among xylophagous beetles.
source: In some regions, the plant extinction was less severe, or the recovery was rapid (Hochuli et al., 2010), or there may have been multiple crises during the Early Triassic (Schneebeli-Hermann et al., 2017), but even short-term ecosystem disruption could have led to extinctions among xylophagous beetles.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the ecological dependence of xylophagous beetles on forests.

claim: Previous studies have not provided a clear picture of insect evolution in response to possible environmental stresses, nor of their response to the EPME.
source: Previous studies have not provided a clear picture of insect evolution in response to possible environmental stresses, nor of their response to the EPME (Benton and Newell, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Benton and Newell, 2014.

claim: The demise of most forests (deforestation event) most likely resulted in the extinction of most Palaeozoic xylophagous beetles, analogous to the extinction of tree-dwelling birds and mammals resulting from end-Cretaceous deforestation.
source: Our results show for the first time that the demise of most forests (deforestation event; Vajda et al., 2020) most likely resulted in the extinction of most Palaeozoic xylophagous beetles, analogous to the extinction of tree-dwelling birds and mammals resulting from end-Cretaceous deforestation (Field et al., 2018; Hughes et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is stated directly in the manuscript and supported by citations to Vajda et al., 2020; Field et al., 2018; and Hughes et al., 2021.

claim: The study reveals an Early Triassic gap in xylophagous beetles, suggesting that early archaic beetles experienced the severe ecological consequences of end-Permian deforestation.
source: Our results reveal an Early Triassic gap in xylophagous beetles, suggesting that early archaic beetles experienced the severe ecological consequences of end-Permian deforestation.
evidence: This claim is stated directly in the manuscript and based on data analysis and inference.

claim: Extant insects are suffering from dramatic declines in abundance and diversity largely due to the anthropogenic deforestation and global warming.
source: Extant insects are suffering from dramatic declines in abundance and diversity largely due to the anthropogenic deforestation and global warming (van Klink et al., 2020; Wagner et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to van Klink et al., 2020 and Wagner et al., 2021.

claim: Xylophagous insects have been largely neglected in studies of the current extinction crisis.
source: However, xylophagous insects have been largely neglected in studies of the current extinction crisis (van Klink et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to van Klink et al., 2020.

claim: The diversity and abundance of xylophagous beetles are extremely sensitive to climate change and can also entail forest collapse and carbon cycle disturbance.
source: In particular, the diversity and abundance of xylophagous beetles are extremely sensitive to climate change and can also entail forest collapse and carbon cycle disturbance (Kurz et al., 2008; Fei et al., 2019; Šamonil et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kurz et al., 2008; Fei et al., 2019; and Šamonil et al., 2020.

claim: The findings may help to better understand future changes in insect diversity and abundance and its consequences faced with global environmental change.
source: Our findings may help to better understand future changes in insect diversity and abundance and its consequences faced with global environmental change.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the implications of the study.
